title: Kollsman Instrument Corp. v. Commissioner
subject: Section 174 Amortization
summary: Kollsman Instrument Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1986-66, aff'd 870 F.2d 89 (2d Cir. 1989), is a U.S. federal tax case for contractors claiming research deductions and R&D tax credits. The Tax Court denied IRC § 174 deductions because Kollsman's production contracts did not require it to invent, develop the concept of, or design any product.

body.text: (1) Executive Summary & Case Background

In the jurisprudence governing United States federal research tax incentives, Kollsman Instrument Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1986-66, 51 T.C.M. (CCH) 463 (1986), aff'd, 870 F.2d 89 (2d Cir. 1989), stands as a foundational precedent delineating the statutory boundary between qualifying research and experimental (R&E) activities and non-qualifying contract manufacturing or routine production engineering. Although litigated under the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 over two issues—the timing of a $4,359,000 deduction claimed on the 1966 return for a loss on a long-term Air Force contract, and whether expenditures of $868,000, $2,114,000, and $1,389,000 claimed for 1966, 1967, and 1968 were currently deductible as research and development costs under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 174 (the 1967 and 1968 amounts being at issue through their effect on the net operating loss (NOL) carryback adjustment for 1965)—and therefore decided on tax years that predate the federal research credit, the decision forms a cornerstone of modern IRC § 41 Research and Development (R&D) tax credit enforcement. Because IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) explicitly incorporates IRC § 174 as the threshold gateway requirement for "qualified research," both the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and federal courts routinely invoke Kollsman Instrument Corp. to disallow R&D tax credits where a taxpayer's underlying commercial or government contracts require the production and delivery of complex hardware rather than the conceptual invention or design of a new or improved product.
Factual Context and the Taxpayer's Claim

The petitioner, Kollsman Instrument Corporation, was a New York corporation that, from its incorporation until December 29, 1972, was a wholly owned subsidiary of Standard Kollsman Industries, Inc., an Illinois corporation, and that became the Kollsman Instrument Company Division of Sun Chemical Corporation on that date, when Standard Kollsman Industries merged into Sun Chemical Corporation pursuant to a plan of reorganization; Kollsman was an established aerospace, avionics, and defense contractor. During the relevant taxable periods, the taxpayer produced aircraft instrumentation under contracts with the United States Air Force, the Department of the Navy, and The Boeing Company—including the Boeing 737 Air Data Computer (the KS-200 Contract), AAU-19 Altimeters for the Air Force, altimeters for the Boeing 747 aircraft (the Boeing 4289 and 4292 Contracts), and the AAU-21A Altimeter for the Navy—and, under separate Air Force contracts, fabricated operational prototypes of, and later manufactured, a geodetic and photo mapping system and a ground data processing subsystem.

In performing these government and commercial contracts during 1966, 1967, and 1968, Kollsman incurred various expenses, a portion of which it treated as research and development costs; the Commissioner later conceded that the expenses were incurred in the amounts claimed and were connected with Kollsman's trade or business. On its federal income tax returns for 1966, 1967, and 1968, the taxpayer deducted $868,000, $2,114,000, and $1,389,000, respectively, as research and development costs under IRC § 174 incurred in the performance of these contracts, while amortizing all of its other expenses over a three-year period; the 1967 and 1968 deductions were in dispute because of their effect on the net operating loss carryback adjustment for 1965. To substantiate its position that the contract activities satisfied the statutory requirements of IRC § 174, Kollsman relied heavily on the underlying government and commercial contracts themselves as primary evidentiary proof that its engineering workforce was engaged in qualified research and development.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

In his notice of deficiency, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue determined an overassessment of $137,840 for 1965 and a deficiency of $2,330,954 for 1966; insofar as relevant to the research issue, he disallowed the $868,000 current deduction claimed for 1966, capitalized that amount over three years (thereby allowing a deduction of $289,000 in 1966), and likewise capitalized the claimed research and development deductions for 1967 and 1968. Before the Tax Court, the Commissioner conceded that Kollsman incurred the expenses in the amounts claimed and that they were connected with its trade or business, but contended that the expenditures were not research and experimental expenditures within the meaning of IRC § 174 and therefore had to be amortized over three years rather than deducted in the year incurred.

Kollsman, for its part, argued that its contracts specifically provided that it perform duties of a research and experimental nature, quoting selectively from those contracts to highlight segments that, read alone, could be interpreted as requiring it to perform design activities, produce prototypes, and engage in pre-operation testing. It was the Tax Court itself—after careful review of the submitted contracts, which included commercial agreements with Boeing as well as Air Force and Navy contracts—that concluded the contracts did not require Kollsman to invent or to develop the concept of or to design any product, and that they could fairly be characterized as production contracts under which Kollsman agreed to manufacture or produce certain equipment in accordance with designs furnished to it.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The dispute in Kollsman Instrument Corp. was decided under IRC § 174 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 and the then-applicable Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a), but its continuing significance lies in the interlocking statutory architecture of IRC § 174 and IRC § 41, along with their corresponding Treasury Regulations and administrative rulings. Under IRC § 174, a taxpayer may treat research and experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year in connection with its trade or business as deductible or amortizable R&E costs rather than standard capital or inventory costs. Because the statute itself does not define "research and experimental expenditures," that definition is supplied by Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), which defines the term as expenditures incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business which represent research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense." Under this regulation and Rev. Rul. 73-275, 1973-1 C.B. 134, qualifying R&E expenditures are strictly limited to investigative costs expended in developing the concept of a model or product and eliminating uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Crucially, Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) dictates that eligibility depends on the nature of the activity to which the expenditures relate, not the nature of the product or improvement being developed or the level of technological advancement the product represents. Furthermore, IRC § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b) explicitly exclude any expenditure for the acquisition or improvement of land or of property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation or depletion.

Originally enacted in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 to incentivize private-sector innovation and subsequently restructured by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 into IRC § 41, the federal R&D tax credit provides an incremental tax credit equal to 20 percent of a taxpayer's Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) exceeding a statutory base amount, alongside 20 percent of basic research payments. Under IRC § 41(b)(1)–(3), QREs comprise in-house research expenses and 65 percent of contract research expenses paid or incurred to non-employees for qualified research. In-house research expenses encompass wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services—defined as engaging in qualified research or engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of qualified research—and amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research. IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) defines supplies as any tangible property other than land, improvements to land, and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation.

To constitute "qualified research" under IRC § 41(d)(1), activities must satisfy a cumulative Four-Part Test applied separately to each business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A). First, under the Section 174 Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), the research must be an activity with respect to which expenditures may be treated as expenses under IRC § 174, a requirement that directly embeds the Kollsman holding into every IRC § 41 R&D credit claim. Second, under the Technological in Nature or Discovery Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, meaning the evaluative process fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the Business Component Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), the application of the discovered technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, defined in IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and § 41(d)(3)(A), substantially all—defined by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as at least 80 percent, measured by cost or another reasonably consistent basis—of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation involving the evaluation of more than one alternative where the capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain at the outset, relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.

Even where technical activities appear complex, Congress enacted strict statutory exclusions in IRC § 41(d)(4) to prevent routine commercial engineering and production from claiming the credit. Most relevant to the Kollsman doctrine are IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), which excludes research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component; IRC § 41(d)(4)(B), which excludes research related to the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need; IRC § 41(d)(4)(F), which excludes research conducted outside the United States; and IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), which excludes "funded research"—any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity, where the taxpayer fails to bear the financial risk of failure or fails to retain substantial rights in the research results. Furthermore, under IRC § 280C(c)(1), section 174 deductions must be reduced by the amount of the IRC § 41 research credit unless the taxpayer elects a reduced credit rate, and as part of the general business credit under IRC § 38, the credit is subject to statutory tax liability limitations.
The Court's Final Holding

In Kollsman Instrument Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1986-66, filed February 11, 1986, the United States Tax Court sustained the Commissioner's disallowance of the IRC § 174 research and experimental deductions, and also sustained his disallowance of the $4,359,000 long-term contract loss deduction claimed for 1966, because Kollsman's appeal of its equitable adjustment claim was still pending at the close of 1966 and the amount was not fixed until the $2,000,000 settlement approved on September 26, 1967. Examining the contracts Kollsman placed in evidence—its Boeing, Air Force, and Navy contracts for an air data computer and altimeters—the Tax Court held that the claimed expenditures were not research and experimental expenditures within the meaning of IRC § 174 and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a) (as then in effect under the 1954 Code) because the contracts did not require Kollsman to invent or to develop the concept of or to design any product. Rather, the court found the contracts could fairly be characterized as production contracts under which Kollsman agreed to manufacture or produce certain equipment in accordance with designs furnished to it, which did not require it to perform duties of an experimental nature; independently, the court held that even if research and experimental expenditures had been incurred under the Boeing contract, the claimed amounts were not broken down in any way to indicate the nature and amount of the expenses, so Kollsman failed to prove either its entitlement to or the amount of its § 174 deductions, and the court declined to apply the Cohan rule to estimate any allowable portion.

On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's decision in Kollsman Instrument Corp. v. Commissioner, 870 F.2d 89 (2d Cir. 1989), upholding the deficiency determinations and addressing the procedural interplay of net operating loss carrybacks from subsequent tax years. In subsequent federal tax jurisprudence—including Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), and IRS Chief Counsel Advice (CCA 200013017)—both the courts and the IRS cite Kollsman and its Fifth Circuit counterpart, Agro Science Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1989-687, aff'd, 927 F.2d 213 (5th Cir. 1991), for the black-letter legal rule that expenditures under contracts that do not require the taxpayer to invent or design a product cannot satisfy IRC § 174 or qualify for the IRC § 41 R&D tax credit.
(2) Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous legal and technical deconstruction of Kollsman Instrument Corp. v. Commissioner reveals that the failures fatal to the taxpayer's claim were a fundamental contractual scope deficiency (the contracts did not require Kollsman to invent or design any product) and a failure to substantiate the nature and amount of the claimed expenditures; read together with later authorities, these failures inform four intersecting compliance themes: the obligation to invent or design, the requirement of research in the experimental or laboratory sense, the separation of conceptual development from commercial production and customer adaptation, and substantiation, cost-segregation, and funded-research risks in government contracting (the production-cutoff and funded-research themes derive from subsequent § 41 authorities rather than from the Kollsman opinion itself).
Contractual Scope Deficiencies and the "Invent or Design" Mandate

The primary legal failure in Kollsman Instrument Corp. originated within the four corners of the agreements the taxpayer introduced into evidence. To prove that its expenditures were research and experimental expenditures, Kollsman quoted extensively—and selectively—from the contracts under which the alleged research and experimental duties were performed, which included commercial agreements with Boeing as well as Air Force and Navy contracts, in a case submitted on stipulated facts and exhibits. However, judicial scrutiny of those contracts revealed that they were production contracts under which Kollsman agreed to manufacture or produce certain equipment in accordance with designs furnished to it, rather than contracts requiring it to invent, develop the concept of, or design any product; several were entered into after Kollsman submitted cost proposals in response to buyer invitations that set forth specifications, priced the items by unit and total price for stated quantities (ranging from 1,201 to 1,576 units in the case of the AAU-19 contract), and set production and delivery schedules, such as Boeing's monthly shipset schedule for the KS-200 Air Data Computer under Detail Specification No. 10-61229.

Under United States tax law, when a taxpayer performs work pursuant to a customer or government contract, the contractual scope of work dictates the legal nature of the expenditures. If a contract provides the baseline architecture, functional schematic, or detailed performance blueprint, and obligates the contractor merely to apply established engineering principles to build, assemble, or refine the hardware to meet acceptance testing, the contractor is legally performing a manufacturing or production service, not R&E under IRC § 174. The Tax Court in Kollsman held that, because the contracts were production contracts that did not require Kollsman to invent, develop the concept of, or design any product or to perform duties of an experimental nature, the claimed expenditures were not deductible as research and experimental expenditures under IRC § 174; the court did not address IRC § 41, which did not apply to the years at issue, and under the Commissioner's determination the costs were amortized over three years rather than deducted currently.
Failure to Prove Technological Uncertainty in the Experimental or Laboratory Sense

Closely tied to the contractual deficiency was Kollsman's inability to satisfy the qualitative threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), which mandates that expenditures represent research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense." Taxpayers operating in advanced industrial sectors—such as aerospace avionics, defense electronics, and precision optics—frequently fall into the analytical trap of assuming that because their products are technologically complex, every engineering hour spent bringing those products to fruition constitutes qualified research.

Treasury regulations adopted after Kollsman, and the IRS, explicitly reject this "high-tech product" fallacy. As codified in Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), whether expenditures qualify as R&E depends strictly on the nature of the activity to which the expenditures relate, not the nature of the product or improvement being developed or the level of technological advancement the product represents. Conversely, the Section 174 Test can be satisfied even if the final product is not technologically revolutionary, or if the advance is evolutionary or already achieved elsewhere outside the public domain, provided the taxpayer's methods in the development process are genuinely experimental and investigative. To qualify in the "experimental or laboratory sense," an activity must be investigative in nature, undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that eliminates fundamental uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the concept of a model or product.

In Kollsman, the record did not describe any particular manufacturing, tolerance, or systems-integration challenges; the court found only that the contracts were production contracts for equipment such as air data computers and altimeters to be manufactured in accordance with designs furnished to Kollsman. However, engineering difficulty or manufacturing complexity is not synonymous with technological uncertainty under IRC §§ 174 and 41. When an experienced aerospace engineer knows at the outset that a system can be built and knows the established engineering methodologies required to build it, the process of calculating tolerances, selecting components, debugging assembly variances, and conducting quality control testing does not eliminate conceptual uncertainty. The Kollsman court did not analyze technological uncertainty as such; it concluded that the contracts did not require Kollsman to perform duties of an experimental nature and that, on the entire record, Kollsman failed to prove that it incurred research and experimental expenditures within the meaning of IRC § 174.
Conflation of Conceptual Development with Commercial Production and Adaptation

A third compliance theme—not adjudicated in Kollsman Instrument Corp. itself, but developed by the Tax Court and the Second Circuit in Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner—is the need to segregate the investigative development of a product or process concept from its subsequent implementation in production. Citing Kollsman Instrument Corp., T.C. Memo. 1986-66, aff'd, 870 F.2d 89 (2d Cir. 1989), the Tax Court in Union Carbide articulated the governing legal principle: if a project involves both the development of the concept of a new or improved product or process and the use or manufacture of that product or process in commercial production, only the expenditures incurred in developing the concept qualify under IRC § 174 and IRC § 41.

In practice, long-term defense and industrial contracts span multiple lifecycle phases, transitioning from early conceptual feasibility studies into pre-production tooling, pilot-line runs, quality assurance testing, and full-scale commercial production. Once the underlying concept of a business component is validated—meaning the fundamental uncertainty regarding capability, method, and appropriate design is resolved—research legally ends for purposes of IRC § 41. Any subsequent engineering activity constitutes either disqualified post-production activity under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), routine quality control and procurement management, or disqualified customer adaptation under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) by adapting an existing engineering design to fit a specific customer's procurement requirements. Furthermore, where contract execution requires fabricating specialized tooling, test benches, or photolithography masks that have a useful life extending beyond the research phase, those costs are disqualified as depreciable property under IRC § 174(c) and IRC § 41(b)(2)(C). Similarly, as held by the Second Circuit in Union Carbide, raw materials or prototype supplies used during experimental runs on products that are manufactured for sale and actually sold—costs that the taxpayer would have incurred regardless of any qualified research—are excluded as indirect expenditures under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1). In Kollsman, the court did not address a concept-versus-production allocation; it held that the contracts were production contracts and, independently, that the claimed amounts were not broken down in any way to indicate the nature and amount of the expenses, so the current § 174 deductions were disallowed in full, although the Commissioner's determination capitalized those amounts and allowed them to be amortized over three years (for example, $289,000 of the $868,000 claimed for 1966).
Substantiation, Nexus, and Funded Research Vulnerabilities in Defense Contracting

Finally, Kollsman Instrument Corp. highlights severe evidentiary pitfalls: the court relied on the rules that deductions are a matter of legislative grace, that the Commissioner's determination is presumptively correct, and that the taxpayer bears the burden of proof (Tax Court Rule 142(a); Welch v. Helvering; New Colonial Ice Co. v. Helvering), rules that today are reinforced by IRC § 6001, Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1, and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), while the Funded Research Exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) presents a separate contractual risk that was not at issue in the case. Under IRC § 6001 and the regulations governing IRC §§ 174 and 41, a taxpayer bears the burden of maintaining sufficiently usable, contemporaneous books and records to substantiate both the qualitative eligibility of its Qualified Research Activities (QRAs) and the quantitative nexus connecting specific QREs (wages, supplies, and contract research) to individual business components.

In Kollsman, the claimed amounts were not broken down in any way to indicate the nature and amount of the expenses; the court was not persuaded by Kollsman's bare assertion that they were research and experimental costs, held that its decision to deduct certain expenses and capitalize others was not conclusive of their character, rejected (distinguishing Weimerskirch v. Commissioner) its argument that the presumption of correctness should not apply because the Commissioner offered no evidence challenging its books and records, and refused to relieve it of its burden of proof on the ground that knowledgeable employees were no longer available—noting that the petition was filed in December 1972 but the case was not submitted until some 11 years later after continuances granted at Kollsman's request (primarily because of a related suit pending in the Court of Claims), without finding that Kollsman had unnecessarily delayed the case. Relying on high-level procurement contracts without contemporaneous R&D project reports, project memoranda, laboratory notebooks, hypothesis-driven test logs, and granular time-tracking records is fatal in Tax Court litigation. As demonstrated in subsequent Tax Court decisions such as Norwest Corp., Eustace, and Shami, generalized testimony or non-contemporaneous expert reports that describe general existing technology or contract deliverables—without addressing the specific technical uncertainties, iterative alternatives evaluated, and time spent on qualified versus non-qualified activities—fail the discovery and process-of-experimentation tests. While courts may occasionally invoke the Cohan rule to estimate allowable credits where qualified research is proven to have occurred (as seen in Union Carbide and Fudim), the Tax Court in Kollsman refused to apply Cohan because the taxpayer had failed to establish that any of its expenses were of the type deductible under § 174 and had presented nothing upon which an approximation could be made, and later courts have likewise refused Cohan relief where taxpayers provide uncorroborated, self-serving time estimates.

Moreover, although the Funded Research Exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) was not at issue in Kollsman—the years involved predated the research credit, and the contracts in question included commercial Boeing agreements as well as Air Force and Navy contracts—federal R&D case law analyses use the case to illustrate the hazards that contract terms can create under that exclusion. Under federal procurement frameworks, if a government or commercial fixed-fee or cost-plus contract reimburses the contractor's costs without conditioning payment on the successful experimental creation of a new product concept, or if standard procurement clauses vest exclusive ownership in the customer so that the taxpayer fails to retain substantial rights in its designs, the research is "funded" and statutorily excluded from IRC § 41. Thus, a defense contractor whose contract fails the Kollsman "invent or design" test simultaneously faces dual disqualification: the work is neither investigative research under IRC § 174 nor unfunded research in which the taxpayer bears financial risk and retains substantial rights under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).
(3) Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement implicated in Kollsman Instrument Corp. v. Commissioner and its progeny against the taxpayer's specific legal and evidentiary failures and the governing judicial standard of proof required by the United States Tax Court and federal appellate courts.

headers: Taxpayer's Failure in Kollsman Instrument Corp.
Judicial Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Mandate

cells: Section 174 Test: "Invent or Design" Conceptual Mandate
Relied on government and commercial equipment contracts that provided existing baseline designs/specifications and did not require the taxpayer to invent or design any new product concept.

The taxpayer must produce explicit contractual provisions or internal project charters proving an affirmative obligation to originate, invent, or design the concept of a new or improved model, product, or process.
Elimination of Uncertainty in the "Experimental or Laboratory Sense"

Quoted selectively from contract segments suggesting design activities, prototypes, and pre-operation testing; the court found the contracts were production contracts that did not require duties of an experimental nature and did not separately analyze conceptual uncertainty regarding capability, method, or design.

Qualification depends on the nature of the activity, not the complexity of the product. The taxpayer must substantiate specific technical uncertainties that could not be resolved through standard engineering knowledge at the outset.
Segregation of Conceptual R&D from Production & Adaptation
IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) (Post-Production); IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) (Adaptation); Union Carbide / Kollsman Doctrine

Claimed lump-sum amounts ($868,000, $2,114,000, and $1,389,000) that were not broken down in any way to indicate the nature and amount of the expenses; the court did not address a concept-versus-production cutoff, which was developed in later authorities such as Union Carbide.

When a project spans both concept development and commercial production, the taxpayer must establish a verifiable technical cutoff (phase-gate) and isolate only investigative costs incurred prior to commercial viability.
Process of Experimentation & "Substantially All" Rule

Not adjudicated in Kollsman (a 1954 Code § 174 case predating § 41); the court found only that Kollsman agreed to manufacture or produce equipment in accordance with designs furnished to it, under contracts that did not require duties of an experimental nature.

The taxpayer must prove through contemporaneous records (modeling, simulation, systematic trial-and-error) that at least 80% of the activities for each business component constituted a scientific process of experimentation.
Exclusion of Depreciable Property & Tooling Costs

Not at issue in Kollsman; the record did not identify the composition of the claimed amounts, and the depreciable-property limitation is drawn from IRC § 174(c) and IRS CCA 200013017 rather than from the Kollsman opinion.

Property of a character subject to depreciation is strictly excluded from § 41 supplies and § 174 expenses. Only non-depreciable tangible supplies consumed or discarded during experimental trials qualify.
Funded Research Exclusion (Financial Risk & Substantial Rights)
IRC § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)

Not at issue in Kollsman (the funded research exclusion did not apply to the years involved); the contracts, which included Boeing commercial agreements as well as Air Force and Navy contracts, set unit and total prices for stated quantities and production and delivery schedules.

The court examines the specific contractual terms to verify that payment is contingent on the success of the research (financial risk) and that the taxpayer retains substantial rights in the resulting technology.
Contemporaneous Substantiation & Cost Accounting Nexus
IRC § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d)

Relied on selectively quoted contracts and a bare assertion that the claimed amounts were research costs; the amounts were not broken down by nature or amount, the split between deducted and capitalized expenses was not conclusive, and the court refused to relieve the burden of proof or apply the Cohan rule.

The taxpayer must retain contemporaneous technical and accounting records linking specific employee hours and supply costs directly to qualified experimental activities on a business-component-by-business-component basis.

body.text: (4) Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal holdings of Kollsman Instrument Corp. v. Commissioner into actionable tax and engineering governance, the following two applied case studies examine realistic industrial scenarios that mirror the exact pitfalls of the ruling. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how a United States taxpayer can restructure its contractual terms, project governance, technical documentation, and cost tracking to survive IRS examination and United States Tax Court scrutiny.
Case Study 1: Aerospace & Defense Avionics Subcontractor (Overcoming the "Build-to-Spec" Government Contract and Funded Research Pitfalls)
Project Scenario and Initial Legal Pitfalls

AeroOptics Defense Corp. ("AeroOptics"), a U.S. C-corporation based in New York, manufactures precision avionics and multifunction phased-array radar subsystems for military aircraft. AeroOptics enters into a $45 million subcontract with a prime defense contractor under an ultimate U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) procurement program to supply 150 units of an airborne electro-optical targeting and radar-warning receiver pod.

Under AeroOptics' initial business practices, the subcontract is drafted as a standard hardware procurement agreement incorporating government performance specifications (MIL-STD environmental and RF parameters) and progress payments tied to cost incurrence. Internally, AeroOptics assigns all engineering, computer-aided design (CAD) layout, environmental qualification testing, and first-article fabrication to a single general ledger contract cost center, claiming $12 million in engineering wages and prototype materials as IRC § 174 R&E expenditures and IRC § 41 QREs.

If audited by the IRS, AeroOptics faces total disallowance under Kollsman Instrument Corp. and IRC § 41(d)(4)(H). First, the subcontract states that AeroOptics is being paid to "manufacture, test, and deliver 150 targeting pods in accordance with Government Interface Control Document (ICD) 402-B," triggering the exact Kollsman holding that the contract does not require the taxpayer to invent or design a new product concept. Second, AeroOptics' single cost center commingles early conceptual RF antenna design with routine pre-production tooling, MIL-STD quality assurance testing, and commercial production of the 150 deliverable units, violating the Kollsman and Union Carbide concept-versus-production rule as well as IRC § 41(d)(4)(A). Third, the progress-payment structure and standard defense procurement unlimited-rights clauses render the entire contract "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring

To overcome the Kollsman contractual trap and the IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) funded research exclusion, AeroOptics' tax counsel and government contracts team must first restructure the agreement prior to execution by bifurcating the procurement into two legally distinct Contract Line Item Numbers (CLINs) or separate contracts. The first line item, CLIN 0001 (Conceptual R&D and Non-Recurring Engineering), must be explicitly titled and drafted as a "Conceptual Invention and System Architecture Design Mandate." The Statement of Work (SOW) for CLIN 0001 must explicitly stipulate that existing off-the-shelf radar designs and the government's baseline ICD cannot achieve the required simultaneous wideband tracking and thermal dissipation thresholds, and that AeroOptics is contractually required to invent and design a novel gallium-nitride (GaN) active electronically scanned array (AESA) architecture and optical stabilization algorithm. To satisfy IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), CLIN 0001 must be structured as a strict Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP) obligation where payment is contingent upon the successful passage of a Critical Design Review (CDR) and prototype flight-test validation, with no unconditioned cost-reimbursement progress payments, thereby placing the full financial risk of conceptual failure on AeroOptics. Furthermore, AeroOptics must negotiate intellectual property terms retaining patent ownership or commercial licensing rights so that AeroOptics retains substantial rights to commercialize or license the underlying GaN AESA technology on other platforms. The second line item, CLIN 0002 (Low-Rate Initial Production and Full-Scale Manufacturing), will then govern the fabrication, assembly, MIL-STD acceptance testing, and delivery of the 150 commercial units once the conceptual design is frozen at CDR, and AeroOptics will intentionally exclude all CLIN 0002 costs from its IRC § 41 R&D credit claim.

In the second step of remediation, to comply with the Kollsman and Union Carbide mandate separating conceptual development from production, AeroOptics must institute a formal Phase-Gate Engineering Governance Policy. Gates 1 through 3 (Conceptual Formulation, Modeling, and Breadboard/Brassboard Prototyping) are governed exclusively under CLIN 0001, where engineering activities focus strictly on developing the concept of the GaN AESA radar module and optical stabilization software. A hard technical cutoff is enforced at Gate 4 (Critical Design Review and Design Freeze): once the working prototype unit successfully passes environmental and RF chamber validation proving that the conceptual design meets all functional specifications, the Chief Engineer signs a formal "Conceptual Uncertainty Resolution Certificate," at which exact timestamp all IRC § 41 Qualified Research Activities cease. During Gates 5 and 6 (Production Tooling, First-Article Qualification, and Volume Manufacturing), all subsequent engineering activities—including procurement, designing manufacturing jigs, resolving supply-chain component tolerances, conducting routine MIL-STD quality control on deliverable pods, and executing Engineering Change Orders (ECOs) for manufacturability—are routed to CLIN 0002 production accounts and excluded from the tax credit computation under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) and (B).

In the third step, because Kollsman and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) dictate that qualification depends on the investigative nature of the activity rather than the complexity of the aerospace product, AeroOptics must mandate contemporaneous "Technical Uncertainty Memoranda" at the inception of Gate 1 for each discrete business component, such as Business Component A (Wideband GaN Transmit/Receive Module) and Business Component B (Electro-Optical Gimbal Stabilization Firmware). Each memorandum must contemporaneously document the exact physical and engineering parameters required (for instance, maintaining less than attenuation and standing wave ratio (SWR) below across a to broadband range within a regulated thermal envelope). The documentation must further explain why known engineering equations, textbook methodologies, and AeroOptics' prior radar designs cannot achieve this result without phase distortion and thermal runaway, and must articulate the specific scientific hypotheses formulated to eliminate this conceptual uncertainty through trials of a working prototype in the experimental or laboratory sense.

In the fourth and final step, to satisfy IRC § 6001, Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), and the 80 percent "substantially all" Process of Experimentation threshold under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), AeroOptics must overhaul its enterprise resource planning (ERP) and engineering tracking systems. AeroOptics replaces its single contract cost center with granular Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) sub-project charge codes mapped directly to each business component and lifecycle gate, separating experimental simulation and prototype testing on the GaN module from production engineering and routine quality assurance. Employees are required to log hours contemporaneously each day against specific experimental tasks, supported by supervisor sign-off, rather than relying on retrospective estimates rejected in cases like Shami and Eustace. Simultaneously, in its engineering repository and laboratory test databases, AeroOptics records the progression of information discovered across every design iteration, finite-element thermal simulation, and anechoic chamber failure. Each log links the specific WBS labor hours and non-depreciable prototype components consumed and scrapped during destructive thermal testing directly to the evaluation of competing technical alternatives, while capitalizing reusable anechoic chamber test fixtures and oscilloscopes as depreciable property under IRC § 174(c) and § 41(b)(2)(C).
Case Study 2: Semiconductor & Integrated Circuit Fabrication (Segregating Conceptual Process/Design R&D from Depreciable Tooling and Commercial Production)
Project Scenario and Initial Legal Pitfalls

SiliconLogic Microdevices Inc. ("SiliconLogic"), a U.S.-based semiconductor developer and specialized manufacturer, enters into commercial supply agreements with enterprise hardware original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to deliver custom Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs). Under its standard workflow, SiliconLogic receives functional logic and pin-out specifications from an OEM customer, designs or adapts the integrated circuit layout, contracts with a third-party photomask shop to manufacture photolithography mask sets, and runs 24 prototype silicon wafers per week through fabrication from "first silicon" until the chip enters volume commercial production with stable manufacturing yields and minimal engineering support.

On its federal tax return, SiliconLogic claims the IRC § 41 R&D credit for 100 percent of the cost of the photolithography mask sets and all 24 weekly wafers run from first silicon through stable volume production, alongside all process and product engineering wages incurred during that entire timeframe.

As detailed directly in IRS Chief Counsel Advice 200013017—which explicitly relies upon Kollsman Instrument Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1986-66, aff'd, 870 F.2d 89 (2d Cir. 1989)—and Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, SiliconLogic's claim suffers from multiple fatal defects. First, where the OEM customer provides the baseline logic schematic and contracts with SiliconLogic to manufacture wafers and package chips according to customer specifications, the contract does not require SiliconLogic to "invent or design any product," disqualifying the activity under IRC § 174 and Kollsman. Second, under IRC § 174(c) and IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), eligible supplies exclude property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation; because the photolithography mask set is a reusable manufacturing tool with a useful life extending into commercial production, it is depreciable property under IRC §§ 167 and 168 and is completely ineligible as a supply QRE. Similarly, the 14 wafers per week that are not destructively tested and are either held as depreciable property or sold to the customer are ineligible under Union Carbide and CCA 200013017. Third, by claiming all engineering wages and wafer runs up until volume production was reached, yield was stable, and minimum engineering support was required, SiliconLogic violated IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) and the Kollsman and Union Carbide rule, as research ends when the chip design and fabrication process concept are validated, long before commercial yield stabilization is completed.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring

To satisfy the Kollsman mandate, SiliconLogic must first separate its commercial wafer-supply agreements from its upfront Non-Recurring Engineering (NRE) design agreements. For custom ASIC projects where SiliconLogic claims product-level R&D, the NRE contract must explicitly state that the customer is providing only high-level system performance targets (such as clock speed, tera-operations per watt, and die-area constraints) and that SiliconLogic is contractually obligated to invent and design the original transistor-level sub-micron circuit topology, clock-tree distribution network, and on-chip power management architecture. Conversely, where a customer furnishes a completed circuit design layout (meaning the customer designed the chip concept), SiliconLogic must refrain from claiming product development QREs for the chip design under Kollsman. Instead, SiliconLogic must define its internal manufacturing process—such as developing a new sub-5nm lithography etching or chemical-vapor deposition process—as a separate proprietary Business Component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B). Because SiliconLogic owns and uses its proprietary fabrication process in its trade or business across multiple customers, its self-initiated investigative research to invent a new fabrication process concept satisfies the Section 174 Test and Business Component Test independently of any customer hardware contract, provided isolated QRA components during scale-up or automation are rigorously separated from general commercial production.

In the second step, to prevent the IRS from disallowing the entire claim for bleeding into commercial production under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) and Kollsman / Union Carbide, SiliconLogic must establish a formal "First-Silicon to Pre-Production Cutoff Protocol." During Phase I (Pre-Tapeout Architecture and Modeling), engineering activities involve 100 percent conceptual design and computer modeling to resolve layout and signal-integrity uncertainties. During Phase II (Experimental Silicon Validation and "First Silicon" Stepping), prototype wafers return from the fabrication line and engineers test whether the physical silicon matches the theoretical models; if a functional logic bug or electromigration failure requires modifying the transistor layout through design changes, the investigative activities to diagnose and redesign the circuit concept remain in Phase II qualified research. A strict statutory cutoff is enforced at Qualification Sign-Off and Production Release: the moment the chip design passes functional verification and reliability qualification—proving the business component meets its basic design specifications and is ready for commercial release—qualified research legally terminates. In Phase III (Commercial Yield Ramp and Volume Production), all subsequent engineering activities dedicated to stabilizing wafer yields, fine-tuning routine fabrication equipment parameters, and manufacturing commercial wafers for sale are strictly segregated and excluded from the IRC § 41 computation.

In the third step, to comply with IRC § 174(c), IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), and the exact holdings of IRS CCA 200013017 and Union Carbide, SiliconLogic must implement strict asset-classification and material-segregation rules. SiliconLogic removes 100 percent of the cost of production photolithography mask sets from its IRC § 41 supply QREs, capitalizing and depreciating them under IRC §§ 167 and 168 because they are property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Next, following the exact analytical framework of IRS CCA 200013017, out of the 24 prototype wafers run per week during the Phase II design-change stage, SiliconLogic isolates the 10 wafers per week that are specifically pulled from the line, tested for each design change during the development process, and discarded. Because those 10 discarded wafers are necessary to perform experimental research to increase the innovative qualities of the chips and are physically scrapped rather than held as depreciable assets or sold, their costs are properly documented and claimed as qualified supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C). Conversely, the remaining 14 wafers per week—and any wafers whose dies are ultimately packaged and sold to customers during commercial production—are strictly excluded from supply QREs in accordance with CCA 200013017 and the Second Circuit's holding in Union Carbide.

In the fourth step, to substantiate the Process of Experimentation Test and nexus requirements under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), SiliconLogic links its Electronic Design Automation (EDA) version-control software and wafer-lot tracking database directly to its tax accounting ledger. Every experimental design change generates a distinct "Design Change Experiment Ticket" that contemporaneously records the specific signal-integrity or timing uncertainty identified on the prior silicon stepping, the competing circuit layout alternatives evaluated, the exact lot and wafer identifiers of the 10 experimental wafers pulled and discarded to test that specific design change (supported by physical scrap-disposal verification logs), and the exact timecard hours of the design and test engineers executing that ticket prior to the Phase III commercial production cutoff.
Summary Matrix of Remedial Governance Across Both Case Studies

cells: Contractual Scope ("Invent or Design")
Hardware supply contracts and purchase orders requiring fabrication to customer/DoD specifications.
Bifurcated NRE/R&D contracts (CLIN 0001) explicitly mandating original conceptual invention and architecture design.
Conceptual R&D vs. Commercial Production
Claiming engineering wages and materials through volume yield stabilization and delivery of commercial units.
Formal Phase-Gate cutoff at Critical Design Review / Silicon Qualification; post-concept production and yield ramp excluded under § 41(d)(4)(A).
Depreciable Tooling vs. Consumable Supplies
Claiming durable photolithography mask sets, reusable test fixtures, and salable prototype runs as § 41 supplies.
Capitalizing mask sets and test benches under § 174(c)/§ 168; claiming only documented, destructively tested, and discarded experimental wafers/prototypes.
Funded Research & Contractual Risk
Cost-plus or unconditioned progress payments with standard government unlimited IP rights.
Firm-Fixed-Price (FFP) R&D milestones contingent on technical success, coupled with retained patent/commercial licensing rights under § 41(d)(4)(H).
Substantiation & Cost Nexus
Relying on overarching procurement contracts and pooled contract cost centers.
Contemporaneous Uncertainty Memoranda, WBS experimental charge codes, EDA/lot-scrap logs, and activity-level time tracking under IRC § 6001.

body.text: (5) Strategic Conclusions for U.S. Tax Practitioners

The enduring lesson of Kollsman Instrument Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1986-66, aff'd, 870 F.2d 89 (2d Cir. 1989), is that technological sophistication in manufacturing is never a substitute for conceptual invention in the experimental or laboratory sense. When advising United States taxpayers on IRC § 174 research and experimental capitalization and amortization compliance and IRC § 41 R&D tax credit claims, legal and technical advisors must treat customer and government contracts as primary evidentiary exhibits that can either anchor or destroy a claim.

By proactively restructuring contracts to explicitly mandate conceptual design and invention, enforcing strict phase-gate cutoffs prior to commercial production, stripping out depreciable tooling and salable inventory costs, and maintaining contemporaneous experimental documentation linked to granular WBS accounting codes, taxpayers can decisively overcome the evidentiary hurdles established in Kollsman and sustain their research tax positions before the IRS and the federal judiciary.

metaDescription: Kollsman Instrument Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1986-66: § 174 deductions denied because production contracts did not require inventing or designing.
